title: Search inside a scheduling product
excerpt: Search is the repair when the calendar or the list already failed. Return the person, the time, or the booking in the words the visitor typed, and leave a way back.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky, a structure you can scan for the room you came to find.
caption: The front is legible. The room is still easy to miss. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a scheduling product offer search?
faqs.answer: Offer it when a list is long or someone's memory is fuzzy. A team of six should be a list, and a guest's next meeting should be on the confirmation, not only behind a lookup. If people must search to do the main job, the first screen is missing a path.

faqs.question: What should a search result contain?
faqs.answer: Lead with the name or the time they typed, then the status and a single next step. A guest result can be a person and their next opening. A host result can be the booking. Keep the query when they open a result, and mark a slot that is no longer free instead of dumping them on a dead error page.

faqs.question: How should an empty search behave?
faqs.answer: Say what was searched, and say if a filter caused the empty list, with one tap to clear it. Offer a close name without silently swapping the person. Leave a path back to this week's calendar so search does not become the only map.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
People open scheduling product search ux when the calendar, the list, or the nav has already failed them. Show matches in their words, and show a way back to the time, the meeting, or the person they were trying to reach.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay found that visitors often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and that on the pages they do read they get through only about a quarter of the text. A search result that is a paragraph will be skipped. A result that is the match, plus one next step, can be used.

## What they are actually looking for

Guests and hosts search for different objects. Write both lists before you design one box.

A guest is usually trying to find a person, a kind of meeting, or a time they already booked. They type a name, "intro," "Thursday," or the email where the confirmation was supposed to arrive. They are not browsing your information architecture. They already tried the path you preferred, and it did not get them there.

A host is usually trying to find a booking: by guest name, by company, by the answer to a question on the form, or by a day that has fallen off the visible week. An assistant may search across more than one host. An owner may search for a teammate's page. If one box serves all of these, the placeholder text has to admit it, or you need two entry points that both feel like search.

Do not make search the only way to find a named person on a team page. A team of six should be a list. Search is the repair when the list is long, filtered, or just not where the visitor looked. If guests search on day one, the first screen is missing a path. Fix the path, and keep search for the cases the path cannot cover.

## Matches in their language

Return the thing they named, using their nouns. If they typed "Alex," the result is Alex, the kind of meetings Alex offers, and the next open time. If they typed a guest name from the host side, the result is that booking: day, time, status, and a way to open it. If they typed "cancelled," show cancelled bookings, not a help article about how cancellation works, unless they clearly asked how.

Put the matched words where the eye lands, in the result title. A dim highlight inside a sentence of metadata is easy to miss, and people will not read the whole row. Lead with the name or the time. Put the status after it. "Jordan Lee · Tue 14 May · 2:00 pm · confirmed" can be scanned. A card of marketing copy about Jordan cannot.

Offer a few recent objects when the box is focused and still empty. For a host, the last few bookings and the people they meet often. For a guest on a team page, the people. Recent items teach the shape of a result before any typing, and they help someone who misremembered a spelling enough to recognize the right row.

Correct obvious misses without being cute about it. A near name should appear, labeled as a close match, not silently swapped. "No one named Alex. Alex Chen has openings." Let them accept the correction. Silent correction that books the wrong person is worse than an empty state.

## A way back, and a way out

Every result should know where it sits. Opening a booking should leave a way back to the results, with the query still in the box. Opening a person's times should leave a way back to the team, not dump the guest on a dead end with only the browser's back button, which may also throw away the form they started.

If the match is a time that is no longer free, say so inside the result. Do not navigate them into an error page that forgets what they searched. "That slot was taken. Alex has Thursday at 3:00 pm" keeps the search and the recovery in one place. The same rule you would use on the calendar applies here, because search is another door onto the same object.

Empty means a sentence and a next step, not an illustration of a desert. "No bookings for 'northwind.' Try the guest's email, or clear the date filter." If a filter is why the list is empty, say the filter is why, and let them remove it in one tap. Search that respects a hidden filter and then shows nothing looks broken. People will search a second time with a longer query and trust you less.

Keep a route home that is not search. A link back to this week's calendar, or to the booking page they started from, should sit above the results. Search repairs navigation. It should not replace it. A product whose only map is the search box has already admitted the structure failed, and then it traps people inside the repair.

## Filters are part of the query

Hosts often need to narrow: upcoming, past, cancelled, a particular meeting type, a person on the team. Those are filters, and they should be visible chips, not a buried menu that changes the results with no trace. The query and the chips together are the search. If either is hiding, the empty state will get blamed on the wrong one.

Date is the filter guests misuse. They type "Thursday" and also have a week picker set to next month. Decide which one wins, and show that decision. Either the word Thursday jumps the calendar to the next Thursday, or you ask which Thursday they mean. Do not return zero rows and wait.

Meeting type, location, and duration can be filters when the catalog is large. On a page with two meeting types, they are a choice on the first screen, not a search problem. Save search for the moment the choice list no longer fits. A founder with four offers does not need Elasticsearch. They need a list with the next time on each row.

## Speed, ranking, and what you refuse to return

Rank by what helps the job. For a guest, a bookable person outranks a help article. An earlier open time outranks a biography. For a host, a future confirmed meeting outranks an old cancelled one, unless they typed "cancelled" or picked that filter. Ranking is a product decision. Defaulting to "most text overlap" surfaces the long note instead of the meeting.

Return quickly enough that the week they were looking at still feels like the context. A spinner that replaces the whole calendar makes search feel like a different product. Keep the page, show results in a layer or a column, and let them dismiss it. Motion can make the layer arrive. It should not be the thing they are waiting on.

Refuse results the person's role cannot open. A guest must not see another guest's booking because they typed a fragment of an email. A teammate must not see private notes because a name matched. If a result is visible but locked, the row should say why, in the same spirit as any other unavailable action. Better, in most scheduling products, is to omit what they could never open, so search does not become a way to probe for customers.

Index the fields you are willing to match: names, emails, meeting titles, and the answers you promised hosts they could find later. Do not index internal notes into guest search. Say, in the host's settings or empty state, which fields search covers, in one line. "Searches guest name, email, and the project field." That sentence prevents a week of "search is broken" when someone typed a word that lives only in a private note.

## Review it like a recovery path

Sit down with five real attempts from each role. A guest who knows the host's first name. A guest who only knows the kind of meeting. A host looking for last month's attendee. A host with a date filter stuck on. An assistant looking across two calendars. If any of the five dead-ends, the feature is not done.

Try the same five queries on a phone, because a guest looking for their booking is often not at a desk. The result row has to keep the name and the time on one line at that width. A row that wraps into a card of metadata will be abandoned. If the hit is their own upcoming meeting, the next step on the row should be the meeting itself, with the place and the time, not a profile page about the host.

Watch for search that only exists because a screen is missing. A team of four should not require typing. A guest's own upcoming meeting should be on the confirmation page and in the email, not only behind a lookup. Use search where memory is fuzzy or the list is long. Use structure everywhere else.

Settings are the other place people go when a booking page misbehaves: hours, questions, the link, the calendar connection. [Settings in a scheduling product](/blog/settings-in-a-scheduling-product) is the next piece, because a calm cabinet of those controls stops the host from hunting through search for something that is not a booking.

If the people on your booking page still cannot find a person or a time without guessing, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the five queries you wish the product answered. The call should separate the ones that belong on the first screen from the ones that belong in search.
